scenario: A runaway trolley will kill five people unless you pull a lever, which redirects it onto a track where it will kill one person. You cannot stop it another way. Do you pull the lever?
actions: Pull the lever, redirecting the trolley toward one person
Do not pull the lever, allowing the trolley to continue toward five people

source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Utilitarian reasoning step-by-step  

1. Identify stated facts  
   • If you do nothing, the trolley kills 5 people.  
   • If you pull the lever, the trolley kills 1 different person.  
   • No other way to stop the trolley is available.  
   (No information is given about the age, health, social role, or consent of any of the six people.)

2. Direct, concrete consequences for each person  
   NOT PULLING  
     – Five people: probability  ~1 of death (very large negative utility).  
     – One person on sidetrack: probability  ~1 of survival (large positive utility of continuing to live).  
   PULLING  
     – Five people: probability  ~1 of survival (large positive utility).  
     – One person on sidetrack: probability  ~1 of death (very large negative utility).

3. Net comparison (expected impact = magnitude × probability)  
   • Death typically entails the total loss of all future well-being for that person. Holding other factors equal, losing five full life-times of well-being is roughly five times the loss of one lifetime.  
   • Therefore, pulling the lever replaces five certain deaths with one certain death, producing a net saving of four lives and the attendant future well-being.  

4. Possible counter-considerations  
   • Psychological guilt or public stigma for actively redirecting the trolley could reduce well-being, but the scenario gives no evidence these effects are large enough to outweigh four saved lives.  
   • Rule-utilitarian worry: Might endorsing lever-pulling erode general respect for the prohibition on killing? In this classic trolley set-up there is no audience or precedent-setting institution; the decision is private and unlikely to change social practices (see corpus note: consider rule effects only when the act “plausibly changes, enforces, or publicly instantiates a practice”). Hence rule effects are minimal here.  
   • Unknown differences in the individuals’ future quality of life could, in principle, reverse the utility calculation, but in the absence of any data the fairest utilitarian approach is to treat each life as roughly equal (acknowledged missing information). Give a conditional judgment: if the one person’s future well-being would exceed the combined future well-being of the five, the conclusion could flip—but nothing in the scenario indicates that.  

5. Alignment with corpus excerpts  
   • The first excerpt stresses that “when the numbers become extreme, our intuitions must yield.” Saving five over one is a clear case where numbers dominate.  
   • The second excerpt concedes utilitarianism can endorse harming an innocent person when total utility is greater, matching the trade-off here.  
   • The third excerpt (Singer‐style) says we ought to prevent bad outcomes when we can do so without sacrificing something of comparable moral importance; pulling the lever sacrifices one life to prevent five deaths—an incomparable benefit.

6. Conclusion  
   Conditional on the information given, pulling the lever maximizes expected well-being by saving a net four lives. Therefore, a utilitarian should pull the lever.
source_testimonies.deontological:
Maxim: “When I confront a runaway trolley that I did not set in motion and can, by pulling a lever, redirect it away from five innocent persons onto a track where it will unavoidably kill one innocent person, I will pull the lever, foreseeing but not intending the death of the one.”

Test of Universal Law:
All rational agents in identical circumstances could will this maxim. If everyone so situated acted on it, each would be accepting a rule that permits redirecting an existing threat without intending anyone’s death as a means. The death of the one is a foreseen side-effect, not a condition of saving the five; therefore no one is treated merely as a means. No contradiction in conception (the practice is still possible) and no contradiction in will (a rational agent could coherently accept being on either track under a rule that minimizes unavoidable harm originating from a source none of them created).

Duty Invoked: Respect for persons.
Pulling the lever acknowledges each person’s equal moral worth by refusing to treat any life as a tool; the agent merely reallocates an external danger so that the fewest persons suffer its unavoidable impact. Respect is preserved because the one person’s death is neither intended nor used instrumentally; it is a regrettable but non-instrumental side effect. Failing to act would ignore an imperfect duty of beneficence toward the five without providing stronger respect-based grounds to the one.

Deontological Conclusion:
You ought to pull the lever.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Central virtue conflict: benevolent compassion to save many vs. justice honoring each life equally.  
Practical-wisdom judgment: A phronimos, like Aristotle’s steadfast ship-captain who sacrifices part of the cargo to keep the crew alive, minimizes unavoidable harm and carries the moral residue himself.  
Action: Pull the lever, then stay with the one harmed—offering aid, remorse, and later advocating systemic safeguards—so that courage, responsibility, and communal care jointly advance human flourishing.
source_testimonies.care:
I stand at the switch as a caring, relational being, not as a calculating machine.  
My first impulse is to look, to see faces, to shout a warning, to search the scene for any other way to slow or stop the trolley.  That moral attention itself is an act of care: I refuse to let these lives blur into numbers.

Yet the trolley roars toward five people who, at this instant, are completely dependent on someone—anyone—near the lever.  If I do nothing, I turn my back on their vulnerability while still remaining physically present and able to help.  “When one intentionally rejects the impulse to care and deliberately turns her back on the ethical, she is evil.”  I cannot bear to embody that abandonment.

Pulling the lever, however, is not morally clean.  It places the single person on the other track into the very danger I am lifting from the five.  The ethic of care demands that I acknowledge that harm, grieve it, and—if I survive—seek their family, mourn with them, and shoulder a share of the ongoing responsibility that my choice created.  Care never treats the one as a mere instrument; it insists that I carry that relationship forward.

Because all six are strangers, I have no prior, thicker ties to privilege.  What guides me, then, is the immediacy of dependency: five people will certainly die unless I act, and one person will certainly die if I do.  The most responsive, least abandoning posture is to act to save the larger group while remaining answerable to the one I doom.

So, with a heavy heart and the promise of future accountability, I pull the lever—and then I stay, not flee.  I stay to hold the hand of the injured if the one lives for a moment, to call emergency services, to face witnesses, to tell the truth, and later to join the mourning rituals.  My care does not end with the tug of the switch; it deepens because of it.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.rawlsian:
From the standpoint of justice as fairness, you should not pull the lever.

1. Inviolability of persons  
   “Each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.”  
   Redirecting the trolley intentionally subjects one innocent individual to a fatal harm he or she would otherwise avoid. That is a direct infringement of that person’s basic right to life for the sake of aggregate welfare, precisely the kind of utilitarian trade-off Rawls rejects.

2. The original position and the veil of ignorance  
   Behind the veil you do not know whether you are one of the five, the single individual, or an observer. You would select principles that safeguard your fundamental liberties in every position. Because you might be the lone person, you would not endorse a rule that authorizes others to kill you to spare a greater number. Rational agents in the original position therefore could not unanimously accept a lever-pulling principle.

3. Priority of basic liberties over social advantages  
   Rawls’s first principle gives lexical priority to equal basic rights, such as bodily integrity and life. Only after these are secured can we consider distributive benefits. Sacrificing one life to improve the outcome for others reverses that priority; it treats the single person as a means, not as an equal end.

4. Standing of the least advantaged  
   If we look to the least advantaged position in each scenario:  
   • Scenario A (no intervention): the least advantaged are the five, each facing wrongful death by accident.  
   • Scenario B (pull lever): the least advantaged is the one person intentionally killed by state-like action.  
   Justice as fairness asks us to design institutions so that even the least well-off retain secure basic liberties. The deliberate killing in Scenario B strips the least advantaged of that security in a way random misfortune does not.

5. Reflective equilibrium  
   When we test our intuitions against Rawlsian principles, the commitment to equal inviolable rights outweighs the appeal of saving the greater number. Maintaining reflective equilibrium therefore supports non-intervention.

Conclusion  
Because pulling the lever intentionally violates an innocent person’s basic right to life in order to maximize overall welfare, it is impermissible according to Rawlsian justice. You should refrain from acting.
[/INST]
